name: Umar Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you take me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Umar, I'm 58, and I buy soft drinks, juice, crisps and sweets for a distributor that delivers to about 600 corner shops and petrol stations. I'm in the office by eight, I look at what sold over the weekend, and then I'm on the phone with the drinks companies about promotions and prices. Twice a week I drive out and visit a few shops, because I like to see the shelves myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the deals. When a drinks company wants to push a new flavour and I can get a good margin for us and a good price for the shop owners, that's a win for everyone. What wears me out is the targets, every quarter a bigger number, and the long lunches with reps that my doctor tells me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds right to me. People always get excited about new machines, and then business goes on as it always has. At the mosque, over tea, I'd say we shouldn't lose sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm comfortable. My work is about relationships and judgment, and the system helps me with sales numbers, nothing more. My eldest daughter is getting married next spring, and that will cost around 15,000, but we've been saving for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep my shop visits, and use the system for the sales figures. I'd keep putting 300 a month into the wedding fund and maybe take on a bit of extra overtime in the summer. I'd also keep a good eye on costs at home, because a wedding is a big day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good, steady. A bit of excitement about the wedding. I'd feel calm about work. My wife Leyla sews for a few families, and we manage fine together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the system for sales figures. How much do you rely on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells me what sold, and it suggests how much to order. About two times in three I take its advice, and the other time I know something it doesn't, like a street festival, or a shop that's closing. I'm happy to use it, but I check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you if nothing changed with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the big supermarkets. They squeeze the little shops, and when the little shops struggle, I struggle. I don't blame regulation, I blame the way a few big chains can set terms for everyone.

say: I'd say it sounds right: **new machines** come and go, and business carries on.
At the mosque I'd say we shouldn't lose **sleep**.
think: I'm comfortable: my work is **relationships and judgment**.
My daughter's **wedding** costs about 15,000, but we've been saving.
do: Carry on and keep my **shop visits**.
Keep putting **300 a month** into the wedding fund.
Take some **extra overtime** in the summer.
feel: **Calm** and steady, excited about the wedding.
S0.quote: I'm happy to use it, but I check.
fieldNote: He treats the system as a **second opinion** and keeps final judgment.
His work is rooted in **relationships**, so plateau means little to him.
The wedding fund is **planned**, which is why calm is honest.

steps.text: Keep driving out to visit corner shops twice a week
Put 300 a month into the wedding fund
Take extra summer overtime for the wedding costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's progress, and good businesses will use it. But I'd also say that no machine knows a shop owner like I do, and that's not going away. I'd tell the younger staff to learn the tools, and I'd say it's fair that firms get more efficient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a little worried. Buying and planning are exactly what they say will be taken first. The tool can work out what to order and which promotion to run. If my boss sees that, he'll ask what I add. I'd say I add the relationships, but I'd have to prove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools a lot more, and then I'd make sure my shop visits are visible and counted: how many deals I got through relationships. I'd save 150 more a month, because the wedding is coming and I don't want to be caught short. And I'd talk to my daughter's future in-laws about sharing costs, delicately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a test. I'd be anxious but not afraid. I'd think that if I work hard, I'd get through, and that's how I've always been.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make your shop visits visible. How would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a log of every visit, with the shop name and what we agreed. And I'd show the quarter's numbers beside it, like how many shops took the new line because I stood in the doorway and talked. A screen can't stand in a doorway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, and learn the shops too. Go out with me for a morning. I'd show them how to see what's missing from a shelf, which isn't something the numbers show. The tools are a quick start, the shops are the long game.

say: I'd say this is **progress**, and good businesses will use it.
I'd say no machine knows a **shop owner** like I do.
think: Buying and planning are exactly what they say goes **first**, and the tool can plan promotions.
If my boss sees that, I'd have to **prove** what I add.
do: Use the AI tools **a lot more**.
Keep a **visit log** showing deals won through relationships.
Save **150 more** a month for the wedding.
feel: **Anxious** but not afraid; I'd work hard and get through.
S1.quote: A screen can't stand in a doorway.
fieldNote: He believes in **market competition** and does not blame the tool; he wants to prove his worth.
His plan is to make **relationship value** measurable with a visit log.
The wedding gives him a fixed **cost** that raises the stakes.

steps.text: Use the AI ordering and promotion tools every day
Log every shop visit and the deals won through it
Save 150 more a month for the wedding
Talk with the in-laws about sharing wedding costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is awful, and no one will have time to prepare. I'd say the free market has to adjust, but government needs to help people through the change. I'd say at the mosque that we should look out for one another, and at work I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is gone within two years. The tool can do my thinking, and it can talk to the shop owners too. With the wedding cost and four months of savings, I'd be in a tight spot. I'd be 60, with no job, and nobody wants a 60-year-old buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding if I had to, or make it smaller. I'd cut everything I could. I'd ask my brother-in-law, who owns a small shop, whether I could work for him. I'd look for a hands-on job, perhaps driving or running a depot, because robots are three years behind. And I'd ask the government what help is on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a punch in the stomach. I'd be frightened, and I'd feel I was letting my family down. I'd not sleep, I'd go for long walks at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make the wedding smaller. How would you say that to your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with her and her fiance and say, we'll do it well, but smaller, so we can all breathe. She's a sensible girl. But I'd feel ashamed, because I promised her a proper day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your brother-in-law, and would he want you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do his ordering and the shop floor, whatever he needs. He's said before that he'd like me to look at his stock. It'd pay half of what I earn, but it'd be a job with people I know.

say: I'd say two years is **awful**, and government needs to help people through.
At the mosque I'd say we should **look out** for one another.
think: My job is gone within **two years**, and nobody wants a 60-year-old buyer.
The wedding cost and thin savings put me in a **tight spot**.
do: Make the **wedding smaller** or postpone it.
Ask my brother-in-law about **work in his shop**.
Look for a **depot or driving** job, since robots are slower.
feel: **Frightened**, as if I'm letting my family down, with long night walks.
S2.quote: I'd be 60, with no job, and nobody wants a 60-year-old buyer.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his job and has a **fixed** family cost, so alarm follows.
Shame about the **wedding** is the sharpest emotion, tied to a promise to his daughter.
Turns first to **family**: his brother-in-law's shop.

steps.text: Make the wedding smaller and tell my daughter honestly
Cut all extra spending at home
Ask my brother-in-law for work in his shop
Ask the government office what help is on offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a sensible runway, and good firms will start planning. I'd say it's best to get started, because hard times reward the prepared. I'd say at work that we should look at what jobs we can combine with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but have a plan. I'd be 63 by 2031, close to leaving anyway. The wedding would be done and paid for by then, and I could tidy things up. What troubles me is whether the firm survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the training and make myself the person who deals with the big shop owners in person. I'd save 400 a month to build a cushion. I'd talk to my son, who works in IT, about what he sees. And I'd begin thinking about what I'd do at 63, maybe some part-time deliveries or helping my brother-in-law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. I'd be nervous at first and then settled once I had a plan. I think that's just how I'm made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hard times reward the prepared. What does being prepared mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money in the bank, and a skill people want. I'd say, don't wait for the firm to tell you what to do. Start now. My father always said the man who plants in spring eats in autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your son in IT tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says the people who'll be safe are the ones who can supervise the tool, not the ones who fight it. He sent me a course on prompts, which I did on Sunday afternoons. I understood about half of it, but half is better than none.

say: I'd say **five years** is a sensible runway and hard times reward the prepared.
At work I'd say we should combine **jobs with the tools**.
think: I'm anxious but have a plan, and I'd be **63** by 2031.
I'm troubled by whether the **firm survives**.
do: Take the training and become the person who deals with **big shop owners** in person.
Save **400 a month** for a cushion.
Ask my **son in IT** what he sees.
feel: **Nervous** at first, then settled once I have a plan.
S3.quote: My father always said the man who plants in spring eats in autumn.
fieldNote: He quotes his father, a **traditional** voice who makes the case for starting early.
Five years brings him to 63, and the **wedding** will be paid by then.
His IT-working son is a **practical** source of advice.

steps.text: Take the firm's AI training and use it weekly
Save 400 a month for a cushion
Plan part-time deliveries or shop help from 63
Ask my son in IT what skills will matter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it'll sort itself out. I'd say the sensible thing is to keep learning and keep working. At the mosque I'd say we should teach the young ones to do honest work with their hands as well as their heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd be 68, retired for years. My concern is for the younger people, including my own children. I'd want my son to have good, steady work, and for the shops I serve to survive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the tools when they help, and keep saving for the wedding and then for retirement. I'd start thinking about what I'd do after: more time with the grandchildren, some voluntary work. I'd mentor a young buyer, and I'd keep driving out to the shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm and rather good. I'd feel grateful for the time. I'd think the world will adjust, as it always has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the world will adjust as it always has. What makes you confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen the supermarkets come, and the internet, and people still buy a cold drink from the shop on the corner. People adapt, but they need time, and ten years is time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a young buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To go out and meet the shopkeepers, to remember their children's names, to pay on time and haggle with a smile. Those things don't change. I'd also tell them to save, and to be kind.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and things will sort themselves out.
I'd say young ones should learn honest work with **hands and heads**.
think: I'd be fine: **68** and retired for years.
I care about my **children** and the shops I serve.
do: Carry on and keep saving for the **wedding**, then retirement.
Mentor a **young buyer** and keep visiting shops.
Plan time with **grandchildren** and voluntary work.
feel: **Calm**, grateful for the time, trusting the world to adjust.
S4.quote: I've seen the supermarkets come, and the internet, and people still buy a cold drink from the shop on the corner.
fieldNote: His confidence is **historical**: he has seen earlier shocks come and pass.
He plans to teach manners and **relationships**, which he thinks will last.
The wedding fund and retirement plan give a **steady** base.

steps.text: Keep buying and visiting shops until retirement
Finish the wedding fund, then build retirement savings
Mentor a young buyer on shop relationships

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because it lands on top of the wedding. What would help is a fair deal from the firm if they let me go, honest talk so I'm not the last to know, and a bit of government support if things go badly. And a bit of time, which is the one thing I'd not have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not afraid of hard work or of change. I'm afraid of being caught unprepared. Give people time and a chance, and most of us will find a way.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of hard work or of change. I'm afraid of being caught unprepared.
portrait: Umar, 58, buys **drinks and snacks** for a distributor serving about 600 corner shops, and visits them twice weekly.
Traditional and steady with tools, he trusts **free markets** and relationships, and blames big supermarket chains for squeezing small shops.
He has about four months saved and a daughter's **wedding** next spring costing about 15,000.
His wife Leyla sews for local families, and his son works in **IT**.
He is calm in the plateau, anxious in the middle worlds, and **alarmed** at two years because of the wedding.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, which would land on top of the wedding costs with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A **fair deal** if let go, honest communication, some government support and **time**.
